content: Six months after randomization and completion of the treatment regimen, outcomes related to active tuberculosis (TB) and adverse events were assessed by independent, blinded review panels consisting of two or three members. Treatment completion was determined based on pill counts during routine follow-up visits. In the pediatric trial, randomization was stratified by country and conducted centrally using a computer-based system. Participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio in blocks of varying lengths (2 to 8) to receive either isoniazid or rifampicin. The pediatric trial's enrollment and randomization process were entirely separate from the adult trials. Among participants randomized to isoniazid, six individuals were lost to follow-up, while five were lost to follow-up in the rifampicin group. This accounted for 3% of the total participants being lost to follow-up. The trial had an open-label design, but endpoints such as active TB and adverse events were adjudicated by independent, blinded panels. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) downgraded the evidence by one level due to the open-label design and the inclusion of some sites with low TB burden. In the pediatric trial, the modified intention-to-treat population included 138 participants in the isoniazid group and 132 in the rifampicin group. Among HIV-positive participants randomized to rifampicin, two did not receive any doses of therapy, resulting in safety population sizes of 130 for rifampicin and 138 for isoniazid. In the rifampicin group, six HIV-positive participants were from the phase 2 trial, and 124 were from the phase 3 trial. All grade 3–5 adverse events in the rifampicin group occurred in the phase 3 trial, with two events leading to permanent discontinuation of the study drug. Only one of these events was deemed possibly or probably related to the study drug. In the isoniazid group, seven HIV-positive participants were from the phase 2 trial, and 131 were from the phase 3 trial. One participant in the phase 2 trial and seven in the phase 3 trial experienced grade 3–5 adverse events leading to permanent discontinuation of the study drug. These events were deemed possibly or probably related to the study drug for one participant in the phase 2 trial and four participants in the phase 3 trial. The World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis preventive treatment (second edition) include a GRADE summary of evidence tables. For people at risk of TB disease, the efficacy and safety of a one-month daily rifapentine plus isoniazid regimen were compared to other recommended TB preventive treatment regimens. The overall quality of evidence was rated as low. The GDG noted that the trial compared the one-month regimen to nine months of isoniazid but did not include comparisons to other regimens, such as six months of isoniazid, which is a widely used standard of care. The GDG also highlighted that inconsistency could not be assessed due to the single trial available, and additional trials would be beneficial. In pregnant and postpartum women with HIV, isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) was compared to no IPT or placebo. Liver function tests were only performed when clinically indicated, potentially influenced by knowledge of IPT receipt. The GDG downgraded the evidence due to these limitations. For individuals in contact with patients with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB), six months of levofloxacin was compared to other regimens or no TB preventive treatment. Two randomized controlled trials conducted in South Africa and Vietnam provided data. The pooled analysis of individual participant data was used to estimate effects. The GDG downgraded the evidence for imprecision and indirectness due to the small sample size and limited data on levofloxacin susceptibility.
